title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: Many real-world networks bipartite: two distinct types nodes, ties forming types, never within . Students enroll courses, countries sign treaties, legislators join committees. adjacency matrix rectangular rather square, row column nodes play fundamentally different roles. ame() (cross-sectional) lame() (longitudinal) support bipartite networks. key difference unipartite case model uses separate latent spaces two node types, connected interaction matrix GG.

GG enters differs cross-sectional longitudinal entry points: ame() (cross-sectional bipartite), GG rank-truncated scaled identity, held fixed MCMC. rotation scaling interaction carried UU VV, identified quantity overall multiplicative term UGV′U G V'. lame() (longitudinal bipartite), sampler draws GG iteration conditional Gaussian, one GG shared across periods (see Time-varying interaction matrix ). either case, row-side positions (UU, shape nrow×Rrown_\text{row} \times R_\text{row}) column-side positions (VV, shape ncol×Rcoln_\text{col} \times R_\text{col}) can chosen different ranks. Two terms absent bipartite setting: dyadic correlation ρ\rho (row actor never also column actor, reciprocal tie correlate), joint covariance aa bb, instead independent variances since describe different types actors.

title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: simulate bipartite network 30 students 20 courses, 2-dimensional latent position; interaction matrix GG determines dimensions combine predict enrollment.
code: # simulate a student-course enrollment network n_students <- 30 n_courses <- 20  # true latent positions (unobserved in practice) U_true <- matrix(rnorm(n_students * 2, 0, 0.8), n_students, 2) V_true <- matrix(rnorm(n_courses * 2, 0, 0.8), n_courses, 2)  # interaction matrix: positive affinity on dimension 1, negative on dimension 2 G_true <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, -1), 2, 2)  # enrollment ties; the negative intercept keeps enrollment near 25-30% eta <- -0.8 + U_true %*% G_true %*% t(V_true) prob <- pnorm(eta) Y_bipartite <- matrix(     rbinom(n_students * n_courses, 1, prob),     n_students,     n_courses )  rownames(Y_bipartite) <- paste0("Student", 1:n_students) colnames(Y_bipartite) <- paste0("Course", 1:n_courses)  cat("Network dimensions:", dim(Y_bipartite), "\n") #> Network dimensions: 30 20 cat("Enrollment rate:", round(mean(Y_bipartite), 2), "\n") #> Enrollment rate: 0.29

title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: Fitting bipartite model requires setting mode = "bipartite" specifying latent dimensions node type separately via R_row R_col. summary shows intercept (included covariates) variance components. fitted object also stores student latent positions (U), course latent positions (V), (fixed) interaction matrix (G), additive effects (APM student activity, BPM course popularity).
code: # two chains by default; summary() ends with the between-chain check fit_cross <- ame(     Y = Y_bipartite,     mode = "bipartite",     R_row = 2, # latent dimensions for students     R_col = 2, # latent dimensions for courses     family = "binary",     burn = 500,     nscan = 2000,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE,     # save thinned U/V draws so latent_positions() reports posterior SDs     posterior_opts = posterior_options(save_UV = TRUE) )  summary(fit_cross) #>  #> ── AME model summary ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Call  #> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + U[i,1:2] %*% G %*% V[j,1:2]', family = 'binary' #>  #> ── Regression coefficients  #>           Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat Threshold #> intercept   -0.793    0.113  -7.022       0   -1.011   -0.578 1.006      1.05 #>               ESS     #> intercept 462.819 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use #>   the credible intervals. #>  #> ── Variance components  #>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold      ESS #> va    0.050    0.022 1.001      1.05  864.628 #> vb    0.059    0.029 1.000      1.05 1022.309 #>   va = row variance, vb = column variance #> • Latent dimensions: 96%, 4% of the latent product #> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity #>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws #>   reach by chance, if larger. #> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: simulate panel user–item networks 5 periods whose latent positions drift via AR(1) process ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9. use normal family continuous outcome; calls fit families. data-generating GG constant across periods, lame() estimates. chunk writes AR(1) stationary-variance form (Ut=ρUt−1+1−ρ2ϵU_t = \rho\,U_{t-1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,\epsilon ϵ∼N(0,)\epsilon \sim N(0, ), marginal variance held 1), sampler reports innovation-variance form (Ut=ρUt−1+ϵU_t = \rho\,U_{t-1} + \epsilon ϵ∼N(0,σuv2)\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)); two coincide σuv2=1−ρ2\sigma_{uv}^2 = 1 - \rho^2.
code:
n_periods <- 5 n_users <- 20 n_items <- 15  true_rho <- 0.9 G_long <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.3, -0.8), 2, 2)  U_t <- vector("list", n_periods) V_t <- vector("list", n_periods) U_t[[1]] <- matrix(rnorm(n_users * 2), n_users, 2) V_t[[1]] <- matrix(rnorm(n_items * 2), n_items, 2) for (t in 2:n_periods) {     U_t[[t]] <- true_rho * U_t[[t - 1]] +         sqrt(1 - true_rho^2) * matrix(rnorm(n_users * 2), n_users, 2)     V_t[[t]] <- true_rho * V_t[[t - 1]] +         sqrt(1 - true_rho^2) * matrix(rnorm(n_items * 2), n_items, 2) }  Y_list <- list() for (t in 1:n_periods) {     eta_t <- U_t[[t]] %*% G_long %*% t(V_t[[t]])     # continuous outcome: the latent term plus Gaussian noise     Y_list[[t]] <- eta_t +         matrix(rnorm(n_users * n_items, 0, 0.5), n_users, n_items)     rownames(Y_list[[t]]) <- paste0("User", 1:n_users)     colnames(Y_list[[t]]) <- paste0("Item", 1:n_items) } names(Y_list) <- paste0("T", 1:n_periods)  cat("Time periods:", length(Y_list), "
") #> Time periods: 5 cat("Dimensions per period:", dim(Y_list[[1]]), "
") #> Dimensions per period: 20 15 cat("Average edge weight:", round(mean(sapply(Y_list, mean)), 2), "
") #> Average edge weight: -0.01 cat("True latent AR(1) coefficient:", true_rho, "
") #> True latent AR(1) coefficient: 0.9

title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: simplest longitudinal model holds latent positions additive effects constant time, pooling periods single, precise estimate per actor.
code: fit_static <- lame(     Y = Y_list,     mode = "bipartite",     R_row = 2,     R_col = 2,     family = "normal",     dynamic_uv = FALSE,     dynamic_ab = FALSE,     burn = 500,     nscan = 2000,     odens = 20,     verbose = FALSE,     plot = FALSE )  summary(fit_static) #>  #> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ────────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Call  #> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + U[i,1:2] %*% G %*% V[j,1:2]', family = 'normal' #>  #> ── Model  #> • Time periods: 5 #> • Family: normal #> • Mode: bipartite #> • Latent dimensions: 91%, 9% of the latent product #> ℹ Static fit: U, V, a and b are shared across the 5 periods, and per-period #> predictions vary through the per-period covariates. `dynamic_uv = TRUE` and #> `dynamic_ab = TRUE` let them vary over time. #>  #> ── Regression coefficients  #>           Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat Threshold #> intercept   -0.011    0.024  -0.457   0.648   -0.056    0.038 1.008      1.05 #>           ESS   #> intercept 400   #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use #>   the credible intervals. #>  #> ── Variance components  #>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold ESS #> va    0.020    0.007 1.001      1.05 400 #> vb    0.021    0.008 1.001      1.05 400 #> ve    0.905    0.034 0.997      1.05 400 #>   va = row variance, vb = column variance, ve = residual variance #> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity #>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws #>   reach by chance, if larger. #> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

The periods are below. #>  #> ── Dynamic coefficients per period  #>            Mean    Min   Max Drift Drift_pct Dynamic #> intercept 0.009 -0.034 0.049 0.082   931.231       Y #>  #> ── intercept by period  #>    Estimate StdError CI_lower CI_upper #> T1    0.044    0.032   -0.025    0.102 #> T2   -0.013    0.032   -0.081    0.041 #> T3   -0.034    0.032   -0.099    0.032 #> T4    0.049    0.037   -0.025    0.122 #> T5   -0.001    0.037   -0.072    0.079 #>  #> ── Variance components  #>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold     ESS #> va    0.017    0.006 1.010      1.05 281.075 #> vb    0.019    0.007 0.998      1.05 330.000 #> ve    0.249    0.010 0.999      1.05 330.000 #>   va = row variance, vb = column variance, ve = residual variance #>   Under `dynamic_ab`, va and vb are the variances of the actor levels; rho_ab #>   and sigma_ab describe the per-period deviations around them. #> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity #>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws #>   reach by chance, if larger. #> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare). cat(sprintf(     "True rho_uv = %.2f | posterior mean = %.3f | 95%% CI = [%.3f, %.3f]\n",     true_rho,     mean(fit_dynamic$rho_uv),     quantile(fit_dynamic$rho_uv, 0.025),     quantile(fit_dynamic$rho_uv, 0.975) )) #> True rho_uv = 0.90 | posterior mean = 0.906 | 95% CI = [0.870, 0.934]

title: Bipartite Network Analysis
text: dynamic model worth added complexity? goodness--fit plots provide one comparison: dynamic model’s posterior-predictive distributions better cover observed statistics, extra flexibility paying . panel observed statistic period solid black line filled points, posterior-predictive median dashed grey line, grey band 95% posterior-predictive credible interval. Gaussian bipartite checks sender heterogeneity, receiver heterogeneity weighted four-cycle dependence (average product centered, standardized values around fully observed rectangles). Compare three fitted period.   following boxplots summarize two degree statistics across periods: SD row means (much users vary activity) SD column means (much items vary popularity).  dynamic model fits data better, clearest evidence per period. residual variance ve falls 0.905 static fit 0.249 dynamic fit, 0.25 noise variance simulated (noise sd 0.5). gof_plot(fit_dynamic) posterior-predictive median follows observed sender heterogeneity moves period period (0.35, 0.49, 0.18, 0.36, 0.37), gof_plot(fit_static) median essentially flat. boxplot averages statistic across five periods within draw (colMeans), shows time-averaged part difference: posterior-predictive medians, dynamic versus static, 0.37 versus 0.38 observed 0.35 row-mean SD, 0.17 versus 0.23 0.14 column-mean SD. judge whether dynamic fit earns complexity, read time-averaged boxplot together ve, per-period gof_plot(), loo::loo_compare().
code: # GOF panels for the static and dynamic fits gof_plot(fit_static) gof_plot(fit_dynamic) gof_static <- fit_static$GOF gof_dynamic <- fit_dynamic$GOF  # time-averaged posterior predictive draws (column 1 is the observed value) extract_ppc <- function(gof, stat) {     mat <- gof[[stat]]     colMeans(mat[, -1, drop = FALSE]) }  # observed values averaged over periods obs_vals <- c(     mean(gof_static$sd.rowmean[, 1]),     mean(gof_static$sd.colmean[, 1]) )  # each model contributes its own number of saved draws ppc_df <- function(gof, model) {     n <- ncol(gof$sd.rowmean) - 1     data.frame(         value = c(extract_ppc(gof, "sd.rowmean"), extract_ppc(gof, "sd.colmean")),         model = model,         statistic = rep(c("Row mean SD", "Column mean SD"), each = n)     ) } gof_df <- rbind(ppc_df(gof_static, "Static"), ppc_df(gof_dynamic, "Dynamic"))  obs_df <- data.frame(     statistic = c("Row mean SD", "Column mean SD"),     observed = obs_vals )  # posterior-predictive medians quoted in the text below ppc_med <- with(gof_df, tapply(value, list(model, statistic), median)) ve_static <- round(mean(fit_static$VC[, "ve"]), 3) ve_dynamic <- round(mean(fit_dynamic$VC[, "ve"]), 3)  ggplot(gof_df, aes(x = model, y = value)) +     geom_boxplot() +     geom_hline(         data = obs_df,         aes(yintercept = observed),         linetype = 2     ) +     facet_wrap(~statistic, scales = "free_y") +     labs(         title = "GOF comparison: static vs dynamic",         subtitle = "Dashed line = observed value",         x = "Model", y = "Simulated statistic"     ) +     theme_bw() +     theme(         panel.border = element_blank(),         axis.line = element_blank(),         axis.ticks = element_blank(),         legend.position = "top",         plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),         strip.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = "black"),         strip.text = element_text(color = "white", hjust = 0)     )

code: # R = 0 is the no-latent-space baseline dims_to_test <- list(     c(0, 0),     c(1, 1),     c(2, 2) )  # observed GOF statistics obs_gof <- gof_stats(Y_bipartite, mode = "bipartite")  gof_results <- list() for (i in seq_along(dims_to_test)) {     fit_temp <- ame(         Y = Y_bipartite,         mode = "bipartite",         R_row = dims_to_test[[i]][1],         R_col = dims_to_test[[i]][2],         family = "binary",         burn = 200,         nscan = 2500,         odens = 5,         verbose = FALSE     )     # one-sided posterior predictive tail probabilities     gof_results[[i]] <- c(         R_row = dims_to_test[[i]][1],         R_col = dims_to_test[[i]][2],         pval_rowmean = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "sd.rowmean"] >= obs_gof["sd.rowmean"]),         pval_colmean = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "sd.colmean"] >= obs_gof["sd.colmean"]),         pval_fourcycles = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "four.cycles"] >= obs_gof["four.cycles"])     ) }  do.call(rbind, gof_results)

title: Your First AME Model
text: Imagine ’re studying friendships high school. data nominated friend, plus information student (gender, race, grade). natural first instinct run logistic regression: sharing gender predict friendship? problem friendships aren’t independent observations. students social (nominate lots friends), popular (receive lots nominations), friendships tend reciprocated: Alice names Bob, Bob likely name Alice. standard regression ignores , standard errors wrong. Additive Multiplicative Effects (AME) model handles dependencies directly. gives actor sender effect (aia_i, social ), receiver effect (bjb_j, popular ), position latent space (uiu_i, vjv_j) captures tends connect beyond covariates explain. additive effects enter ai+bja_i + b_j; latent positions enter multiplicatively dot product ui′vju_i'v_j. Think regression takes network structure seriously.

title: Your First AME Model
text: ’ll analyze friendship network Add Health study, longitudinal study adolescents United States. addhealthc3 dataset lame contains directed friendship nomination network along student characteristics. Notice na.rm = TRUE calls: diagonal NA self-ties undefined. NAs stay matrix ame() treats dyads unobserved, filling data augmentation. dyad missing covariate treated way. Two 32 students file recorded race, every dyad belong unobserved; analysis uses 30. modeling: much students vary number friends?  students much social others, much popular – exactly sender receiver random effects capture.
code:
library(lame) library(ggplot2) set.seed(6886)  # load the Add Health friendship network data(addhealthc3)  # binary friendship: any nomination counts Y <- (addhealthc3$Y > 0) * 1 X_nodes <- addhealthc3$X  # keep the students whose covariates are all recorded has_covs <- complete.cases(X_nodes) Y <- Y[has_covs, has_covs] X_nodes <- X_nodes[has_covs, ]  n <- nrow(Y) cat("Students:", n, "
") #> Students: 30 cat("Friendships:", sum(Y, na.rm = TRUE), "
") #> Friendships: 113 cat("Network density:", round(mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "
") #> Network density: 0.13 out_degree <- rowSums(Y, na.rm = TRUE) in_degree <- colSums(Y, na.rm = TRUE)  degree_df <- data.frame(     Degree = c(out_degree, in_degree),     Type = rep(c("Nominations sent", "Nominations received"), each = n) )  ggplot(degree_df, aes(x = Degree)) +     geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +     facet_wrap(~Type, ncol = 2) +     labs(x = "Number of ties", y = "Count") +     theme_bw() +     theme(         panel.border = element_blank(),         axis.line = element_blank(),         axis.ticks = element_blank(),         legend.position = "top",         plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),         strip.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = "black"),         strip.text = element_text(color = "white", hjust = 0)     )

what: A note for ERGM users: what AME assumes
title: Your First AME Model
text: ’re coming ergm / statnet, key difference dependence assumption. ERGM uses change statistics (e.g. gwesp, triangle, kstar) encode unconditional higher-order dependence: changing one tie shifts probability ties directly. AME instead assumes conditional dyadic independence: given additive effects (ai,bj)(a_i, b_j), latent positions (ui,vj)(u_i, v_j), dyadic correlation ρ\rho, covariates, dyads independent, higher-order structure captured indirectly integrating latent effects. Three practical consequences: degeneracy. AME avoids model-degeneracy failure modes ERGMs triangle unconstrained kstar terms. change-statistic interpretation β\beta. coefficient same_grade partial association probit-latent scale, log-odds change conditional rest network. Check dependence summaries need. Joint posterior predictive checks assess whether chosen rank covariates reproduce observed clustering network summaries.
code: fit <- ame(     Y,     Xdyad = Xdyad,     Xrow = Xrow,     Xcol = Xcol,     R = 2, # 2D latent space     family = "binary", # probit model for 0/1 data     rvar = TRUE, # sender random effects     cvar = TRUE, # receiver random effects     dcor = TRUE, # dyadic correlation (reciprocity)     verbose = FALSE,     posterior_opts = posterior_options(         save_ab = TRUE, save_UV = TRUE,         thin_ab = 1, thin_UV = 1     ),     gof = TRUE )

See ?gof_plot statistics = ... aliases exact column names stored fit$GOF. observed values sender receiver degree heterogeneity dyadic dependence (essentially empirical reciprocity) fall inside posterior-predictive histograms: random effects, variance components, ρ\rho model three features directly. Triangle closure term AME model; latent positions reproduce clustering uiu_i vjv_j. share simulated networks observed value 0.15 triadic dependence 0.17 transitivity, observed values lie inside central 95 percent simulated ones. Comparing two panels across values R shows much closure added latent dimension accounts ; triangle closure estimand, ERGM closure term models directly. can also compute GOF fact using gof() function, accepts custom statistics. built-trans.dep panel correlation-style clustering measure; ERGM users typically want raw clustering coefficient (sna::gtrans, scalar summary gwesp(decay = 0, fixed = TRUE) targets), takes lines custom stat: Read way read ergm::gof(): pp_p_right fraction simulated networks observed value, value near 0 means model -predicts statistic. 0.26 across 50 joint posterior replicates. replicates retain uncertainty actor effects latent positions well regression coefficients. See ?gof adding custom statistics (raw triangle counts, degree assortativity, ).
code: gof_plot(fit) # clustering coefficient: transitive triples over two-paths trans_ratio <- function(Y) {     Yb <- Y; Yb[is.na(Yb)] <- 0 # missing ties count as 0     YY <- Yb %*% Yb     triangles <- sum(YY * Yb) # transitive triples     two_path <- sum(YY) - sum(diag(YY)) # two-paths (potential triangles)     c(trans_ratio = triangles / max(two_path, 1)) }  gof_custom <- gof(fit, custom_gof = trans_ratio, nsim = 50, verbose = FALSE) obs <- gof_custom[1, "trans_ratio"] sim <- gof_custom[-1, "trans_ratio"]  # posterior predictive p-value (right tail): near 0 means under-predicted c(     observed = round(obs, 3),     sim_mean = round(mean(sim), 3),     pp_p_right = round(mean(sim >= obs), 3) ) #>   observed   sim_mean pp_p_right  #>      0.485      0.449      0.260

code: # 80/20 stratified mask of off-diagonal dyads set.seed(6886) off_diag <- which(row(Y) != col(Y) & !is.na(Y)) pos_idx <- off_diag[Y[off_diag] == 1] neg_idx <- off_diag[Y[off_diag] == 0] test_idx <- c(     sample(pos_idx, round(0.2 * length(pos_idx))),     sample(neg_idx, round(0.2 * length(neg_idx))) )  Y_train <- Y Y_train[test_idx] <- NA # mask test dyads from the likelihood  fit_train <- ame(     Y_train,     Xdyad = Xdyad,     Xrow = Xrow,     Xcol = Xcol,     R = 2,     family = "binary",     rvar = TRUE,     cvar = TRUE,     dcor = TRUE,     verbose = FALSE,     gof = FALSE )  pred_train <- predict(fit_train, type = "response")  # evaluate_heldout() scores the predictions on a logical test mask test_mask <- matrix(     FALSE,     nrow(Y),     ncol(Y),     dimnames = dimnames(Y) ) test_mask[test_idx] <- TRUE heldout_metrics <- evaluate_heldout(     y_obs = Y,     y_pred = pred_train,     mask = test_mask,     family = "binary" ) heldout_metrics #>   n_eval     auroc     auprc      brier   logloss #> 1    174 0.9231212 0.6893068 0.06925327 0.2208384 cat(     "Test dyads:",     length(test_idx),     " | positives:",     sum(Y[test_idx] == 1),     "\n" ) #> Test dyads: 174  | positives: 23

code: # five stratified folds over the dyads, the same for both models set.seed(6886) scored <- which(row(Y) != col(Y)) fold <- integer(length(Y)) for (v in 0:1) {     idx <- scored[Y[scored] == v]     fold[idx] <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(idx))) }  # fit one model with a fold masked, then score that fold score_fold <- function(k, R) {     Y_k <- Y     Y_k[fold == k] <- NA     fit_k <- ame(         Y_k,         Xdyad = Xdyad,         Xrow = Xrow,         Xcol = Xcol,         R = R,         family = "binary",         gof = FALSE,         verbose = FALSE     )     m <- evaluate_heldout(         y_obs = Y,         y_pred = predict(fit_k, type = "response"),         mask = matrix(fold == k, nrow(Y), dimnames = dimnames(Y)),         family = "binary"     )     data.frame(R = R, fold = k, m[c("n_eval", "auroc", "auprc", "logloss")]) } cv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 2), function(R) {     do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, score_fold, R = R)) }))  # mean ranking metrics over the folds, and the log score summed over the held-out dyads cv$log_score <- -cv$logloss * cv$n_eval aggregate(cbind(auroc, auprc) ~ R, data = cv, FUN = mean) aggregate(log_score ~ R, data = cv, FUN = sum)

title: Dynamic Effects in Longitudinal AME Models
text: Networks change. Allies drift apart, tastes evolve. standard AME model pools across time, assuming actor fixed latent position fixed additive effects every period. lame package provides three mechanisms relaxing assumption: dynamic_uv time-varying latent positions, dynamic_ab time-varying additive effects, dynamic_beta time-varying regression coefficients. vignette explains option , use , interpret results.

title: Dynamic Effects in Longitudinal AME Models
text: standard AME model longitudinal data, tie actors ii jj time tt : yij,t=β′xij,t+ai+bj+ui′vj+ϵij,ty_{ij,t} = \beta'x_{ij,t} + a_i + b_j + u_i'v_j + \epsilon_{ij,t} covariates (xij,tx_{ij,t}) can vary time, sender effect aia_i, receiver effect bjb_j, latent positions uiu_i vjv_j constant: model assumes country’s position latent “sanctioning space” 1993 2000.

title: Dynamic Effects in Longitudinal AME Models
text: set dynamic_uv = TRUE, actor’s latent position evolves time according AR(1) process: Ui,k,t=ρuvUi,k,t−1+ϵi,k,t,ϵi,k,t∼N(0,σuv2)U_{,k,t} = \rho_{uv} \, U_{,k,t-1} + \epsilon_{,k,t}, \quad \epsilon_{,k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)Vj,k,t=ρuvVj,k,t−1+ηj,k,t,ηj,k,t∼N(0,σuv2)V_{j,k,t} = \rho_{uv} \, V_{j,k,t-1} + \eta_{j,k,t}, \quad \eta_{j,k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2) Note innovation parameterisation: σuv2\sigma_{uv}^2 variance period--period innovation, marginal/stationary variance Ui,k,tU_{,k,t} (σuv2/(1−ρuv2)\sigma_{uv}^2 / (1 - \rho_{uv}^2)), fit$sigma_uv holds posterior draws innovation standard deviation. symmetric fits estimated: unit-variance gauge fixes σuv=1−ρuv2\sigma_{uv} = \sqrt{1 - \rho_{uv}^2}, fit$sigma_uv function ρuv\rho_{uv} draws. autoregressive parameter ρuv\rho_{uv}, estimated data, controls persistence: near 1 means positions change slowly, near 0 means essentially re-drawn period. Use underlying community structure evolving – alliances shift, trading blocs realign.

for inference use #>   the credible intervals. #> ℹ intercept is a coefficient path: the row gives the mean level over the #>   periods and its interval, with no z or p-value. The periods are below. #>  #> ── Dynamic coefficients per period  #>             Mean    Min    Max Drift Drift_pct Dynamic #> intercept -1.039 -1.183 -0.806 0.376    36.234       Y #>  #> ── intercept by period  #>    Estimate StdError CI_lower CI_upper #> t1   -0.806    0.099   -1.010   -0.618 #> t2   -1.017    0.087   -1.182   -0.843 #> t3   -1.096    0.086   -1.286   -0.938 #> t4   -1.183    0.080   -1.336   -1.030 #> t5   -1.094    0.087   -1.259   -0.934 #>  #> ── Variance components  #>     Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold     ESS #> va     0.073    0.030 1.001      1.05 422.050 #> cab   -0.005    0.019 1.002      1.05 456.707 #> vb     0.067    0.025 0.998      1.05 452.698 #> rho   -0.148    0.096 1.009      1.05 314.102 #>   va = sender variance, cab = sender-receiver covariance, vb = receiver #>   variance, rho = dyadic correlation #>   Under `dynamic_ab`, va and vb are the variances of the actor levels; rho_ab #>   and sigma_ab describe the per-period deviations around them. #> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity #>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws #>   reach by chance, if larger. #> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare). uv_plot(     fit_dyn_real,     plot_type = "trajectory",     highlight = c("A1", "A5", "A10", "A15") ) trace_plot(fit_dyn_real, exclude = "Error variance")

text: natural workflow fit several specifications compare goodness--fit. use independent data , dynamic effects add nothing. specification compute posterior predictive p-values (often simulated statistics exceed observed): values near 0.5 indicate good fit; values pinned near 0 1 flag statistic model systematically - -generates. sd.rowmean sd.colmean sit near 1 every specification: data generated without actor heterogeneity, four models carry additive effects. specifications compared dyad.dep, cycle.dep, trans.dep columns. every value lies 0.25 0.62, away 0 1: specification reproduces dependence statistics, dynamic terms add nothing static fit, expected data generated without temporal structure. four fits nscan = 2000, burn = 500, odens = 25 give values 0.28 0.56 three columns.
code: # the four specifications on the same data fit_static <- lame(     Y_list,     R = 2,     family = "binary",     burn = 30,     nscan = 150,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE,     plot = FALSE )  fit_uv <- lame(     Y_list,     R = 2,     dynamic_uv = TRUE,     family = "binary",     burn = 30,     nscan = 150,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE,     plot = FALSE )  fit_ab <- lame(     Y_list,     R = 2,     dynamic_ab = TRUE,     family = "binary",     burn = 30,     nscan = 150,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE,     plot = FALSE )  fit_full <- lame(     Y_list,     R = 2,     dynamic_uv = TRUE,     dynamic_ab = TRUE,     family = "binary",     burn = 30,     nscan = 150,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE,     plot = FALSE ) # posterior predictive p-values for each GOF statistic compute_pvals <- function(fit) {     gof <- fit$GOF     sapply(names(gof), function(stat) {         mat <- gof[[stat]]         obs <- mat[, 1] # first column = observed         sims <- mat[, -1] # remaining = posterior predictive         mean(colMeans(sims) >= mean(obs))     }) }  gof_comparison <- rbind(     Static = compute_pvals(fit_static),     Dynamic_UV = compute_pvals(fit_uv),     Dynamic_AB = compute_pvals(fit_ab),     Full = compute_pvals(fit_full) ) round(gof_comparison, 3) #>            sd.rowmean sd.colmean dyad.dep cycle.dep trans.dep #> Static          0.900      0.983    0.517     0.600     0.250 #> Dynamic_UV      0.900      0.950    0.567     0.583     0.400 #> Dynamic_AB      0.917      1.000    0.617     0.600     0.267 #> Full            1.000      1.000    0.583     0.567     0.467

The intercept, a and b carry the grand, row and #> column means of the latent product, as ame() reports them; fit$eb$population #> keeps the population intercept. #>  #> Laplace standard errors (penalised Fisher information, empirical-Bayes #> actor-effect prior): #> intercept   Xd_dyad  #>    0.1116    0.0264  #> Posterior sds of the reported actor effects, positions and product cells (delta #> method under the joint Laplace covariance): `fit$a_sd`, `fit$b_sd`, `fit$U_sd`, #> `fit$V_sd`, `fit$UVPM_sd`; `latent_positions()` reports them as `posterior_sd`. round(cbind(truth = c(0.5, 0.8), estimate = coef(fit), confint(fit)), 3) #>           truth estimate  2.5% 97.5% #> intercept   0.5    0.610 0.391 0.828 #> Xd_dyad     0.8    0.795 0.743 0.847 round(fit$VC, 3) #>    va   cab    vb   rho    ve  #> 0.203 0.034 0.199 0.018 1.095

code: data(YX_bin_list) Yl <- lapply(YX_bin_list$Y, function(y) 1 * (y > 0)) lf <- lame_als(Yl, Xdyad = YX_bin_list$X, R = 2, family = "binary", verbose = FALSE) round(cbind(estimate = coef(lf), confint(lf)), 3) #>            estimate  2.5% 97.5% #> intercept     0.118 0.060 0.175 #> dyad1_dyad    0.754 0.714 0.795 #> dyad2_dyad    0.913 0.866 0.959 #> dyad3_dyad    1.136 1.080 1.192 set.seed(7) nn <- 30; Tn <- 8 nmn <- paste0("a", sprintf("%02d", 1:nn)) # an actor level plus an AR(1) deviation in each period ar1_paths <- function() {     level <- rnorm(nn, 0, 0.6)     dev <- matrix(0, nn, Tn)     dev[, 1] <- rnorm(nn, 0, 0.3 / sqrt(1 - 0.7^2))     for (t in 2:Tn) dev[, t] <- 0.7 * dev[, t - 1] + rnorm(nn, 0, 0.3)     level + dev } an <- ar1_paths(); bn <- ar1_paths() xn <- lapply(     seq_len(Tn),     function(t)         array(rnorm(nn * nn), c(nn, nn, 1), dimnames = list(nmn, nmn, "x")) ) Yn <- lapply(seq_len(Tn), function(t) {     m <- 0.3 + 0.7 * xn[[t]][, , 1] + outer(an[, t], bn[, t], "+") +         matrix(rnorm(nn * nn, 0, 0.8), nn)     diag(m) <- NA     dimnames(m) <- list(nmn, nmn)     m }) fn <- lame(     Yn,     Xdyad = xn,     family = "normal",     method = "als",     dynamic_ab = TRUE,     verbose = FALSE ) round(confint(fn)["x_dyad", ], 3) #>  2.5% 97.5%  #> 0.679 0.717 round(c(ve = fn$VC[["ve"]]), 2) #>   ve  #> 0.65 # estimated sender and receiver paths against the generating ones round(c(sender = cor(c(fn$a_dynamic), c(an)), receiver = cor(c(fn$b_dynamic), c(bn))), 3) #>   sender receiver  #>    0.981    0.985

title: Forecasting Longitudinal Networks with lame
text: simulate 30 actors 6 periods, single dyadic covariate trade, directed binary outcome cooperation. effect trade cooperation time-varying mean-reverting simulation: follows AR(1) around 0.5 persistence 0.7, starting high (0.9) settling toward long-run level. network moderately dense (~37%), 300 ties period. dynamic_beta estimates one coefficient per period, ties period inform coefficient. estimated path follows simulated one: starts high settles toward long-run level, largest gap two 0.07. lame() ran two independently seeded chains compared returning fit; largest R-hat among monitored quantities 1.02. summary(fit) reports posterior persistence ρβ\rho_\beta, Step 5 uses choose transition model.
code: library(lame) set.seed(2026)  n_fc <- 30 T_fc <- 6 rho_true <- 0.7 beta_bar <- 0.5 beta_t_true <- numeric(T_fc) beta_t_true[1] <- 0.9 for (t in 2:T_fc) {     beta_t_true[t] <- beta_bar + rho_true * (beta_t_true[t - 1] - beta_bar) +         rnorm(1, 0, 0.15) }  Xdyad <- lapply(seq_len(T_fc), function(t) {     x <- matrix(rnorm(n_fc * n_fc), n_fc, n_fc)     array(         x,         dim = c(n_fc, n_fc, 1),         dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, "trade")     ) }) a_fc <- rnorm(n_fc, 0, 0.4) b_fc <- rnorm(n_fc, 0, 0.4) Y <- lapply(seq_len(T_fc), function(t) {     eta <- -0.5 + beta_t_true[t] * Xdyad[[t]][, , 1] + outer(a_fc, b_fc, "+")     Yt <- matrix(rbinom(n_fc * n_fc, 1, pnorm(eta)), n_fc, n_fc)     diag(Yt) <- NA     rownames(Yt) <- colnames(Yt) <- sprintf("a%02d", seq_len(n_fc))     Yt }) names(Y) <- paste0("t", seq_len(T_fc))  round(beta_t_true, 3) # simulated coefficient path #> [1] 0.900 0.858 0.589 0.583 0.545 0.432 sapply(Y, function(y) round(mean(y, na.rm = TRUE), 3)) # per-period density #>    t1    t2    t3    t4    t5    t6  #> 0.400 0.374 0.378 0.367 0.352 0.357  fit <- lame(     Y,     Xdyad = Xdyad,     family = "binary",     R = 0,     dynamic_beta = "dyad", # the trade coefficient is AR(1)     dynamic_beta_kind = "ar1", # mean-reverting; switch to "rw1" for drift     nscan = 300,     burn = 30,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE )  # estimated path of the trade coefficient coef_path <- coef(fit) trade_row <- grep("^trade[._]dyad$|trade", rownames(coef_path), value = TRUE)[1] round(coef_path[trade_row, ], 3) #>    t1    t2    t3    t4    t5    t6  #> 0.879 0.824 0.597 0.520 0.520 0.505

code: set.seed(2026) n_sp <- 20 T_sp <- 4 beta_drift <- c(0.4, 0.9, 1.4, 1.9) # drifts upward without mean reversion X_sp <- lapply(seq_len(T_sp), function(t) {     x <- matrix(rnorm(n_sp * n_sp), n_sp, n_sp)     array(         x,         dim = c(n_sp, n_sp, 1),         dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, "sanction_risk")     ) }) Y_sp <- lapply(seq_len(T_sp), function(t) {     eta <- -2 + beta_drift[t] * X_sp[[t]][, , 1]     Yt <- matrix(rbinom(n_sp * n_sp, 1, pnorm(eta)), n_sp, n_sp)     diag(Yt) <- NA     rownames(Yt) <- colnames(Yt) <- sprintf("s%02d", seq_len(n_sp))     Yt }) names(Y_sp) <- paste0("t", seq_len(T_sp)) sapply(Y_sp, function(y) round(mean(y, na.rm = TRUE), 3)) # sparse early on #>    t1    t2    t3    t4  #> 0.034 0.055 0.118 0.161  fit_drift <- lapply(c(ar1 = "ar1", rw1 = "rw1"), function(kind) {     lame(         Y_sp,         Xdyad = X_sp,         family = "binary",         R = 0,         dcor = FALSE,         dynamic_beta = "dyad",         dynamic_beta_kind = kind,         nscan = 250,         burn = 50,         odens = 5,         verbose = FALSE     ) }) # estimated coefficient path under each transition model round(t(sapply(fit_drift, function(f) coef(f)["sanction_risk_dyad", ])), 3) #>        t1    t2    t3    t4 #> ar1 0.471 0.854 1.404 1.862 #> rw1 0.514 0.842 1.404 1.873 x_at <- function(value) {     lapply(seq_len(6), function(h) {         array(             value,             dim = c(n_sp, n_sp, 1),             dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, "sanction_risk")         )     }) } # the same seed gives both forecasts the same coefficient draws beta_forecast <- function(f) {     set.seed(1)     fc_one <- predict(f, h = 6, type = "link", newdata = x_at(1))     set.seed(1)     fc_zero <- predict(f, h = 6, type = "link", newdata = x_at(0))     mapply(function(a, b) mean(a - b, na.rm = TRUE), fc_one, fc_zero) } beta_fc <- sapply(fit_drift, beta_forecast) round(t(beta_fc), 3) #>      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6] #> ar1 1.660 1.500 1.361 1.288 1.193 1.151 #> rw1 1.861 1.849 1.816 1.833 1.790 1.821  drift_df <- data.frame(     h = rep(seq_len(6), 2),     model = rep(c("AR(1)", "RW1"), each = 6),     coefficient = c(beta_fc[, "ar1"], beta_fc[, "rw1"]) ) ggplot(drift_df, aes(h, coefficient, linetype = model)) +     geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) +     labs(         title = "Forecast coefficient by horizon",         x = "Forecast horizon h", y = "Coefficient on sanction_risk"     ) +     theme_bw(base_size = 9) +     theme(         panel.border = element_blank(),         axis.line = element_blank(),         axis.ticks = element_blank(),         legend.position = "top",         plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0),         plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),         legend.title = element_blank()     ) # refit before each of the last two periods and score that period # seed the forecast draws inside lfo() set.seed(1) T_fit <- length(fit$YPM) lfo_periods <- tail(seq_len(T_fit), max(1L, min(2L, T_fit - 2L))) lfo_res <- lfo(     fit,     periods = lfo_periods,     refit = TRUE,     nscan = 500,     burn = 100,     odens = 5,     verbose = FALSE ) print(lfo_res) #>  #> ── Exact rolling-origin LFO ── #>  #> Periods evaluated: 5 and 6 #> Refit per leave-out: TRUE #> Total elpd_lfo: -955.34 #>  period      elpd n_obs #>       5 -481.7928   870 #>       6 -473.5436   870

title: lame Overview
text: lame package provides tools fitting Longitudinal Additive Multiplicative Effects models network data observed time. study relationships actors (countries trading , legislators co-sponsoring bills, students forming friendships across semesters) repeated observations relationships, lame designed . modeling approach builds Additive Multiplicative Effects (AME) framework developed Peter Hoff, whose amen package provides foundational cross-sectional implementation. lame extends framework : Longitudinal data: panel networks observed across multiple time periods, potentially actors entering leaving sample. Dynamic effects: latent positions baseline activity levels can evolve via AR(1) processes (dynamic_uv dynamic_ab). C++ acceleration: core sampling routines Rcpp/RcppArmadillo. Bipartite networks: two-mode networks (e.g., countries treaties) separate latent spaces row column nodes. ggplot2-based diagnostics: trace_plot, gof_plot, ab_plot, uv_plot return standard ggplot2 figures can theme extend. Standard S3 methods: coef(), confint(), fitted(), residuals(), predict(), simulate() work expect R model object. package works netify data preparation.

text: see lame works practice, analyze Dutch college friendship network (van de Bunt, van Duijn, Snijders 1999), panel 32 students arrived strangers rated ’s friendship seven time points. (drop cold-start first wave, students barely knew almost ties exist; six waves remain.) substantive question whether students sort gender, smoking status, academic program, whether residual clustering remains covariates absorbed. dataset includes: Y: directed friendship ratings -1 4 scale (-1 negative/troubled relationship, 0 uncertain tie, 1-4 increasing friendship). binarize positive rating tie ((Y > 0) * 1), rare -1 ratings fold 0 “tie”. X: three node-level attributes: male, smoker, program. construct three dyadic homophily indicators node attributes: same_male, same_smoker, same_program. friendship network’s average density rises across panel students settle , though trajectory monotone (density bounces roughly 0.40 0.63 across six waves):
code: library(lame) library(ggplot2) set.seed(6886)  data("dutchcollege")  n <- nrow(dutchcollege$Y) T_all <- dim(dutchcollege$Y)[3] actor_names <- sprintf("S%02d", seq_len(n))  # binarize and drop the cold-start wave (t = 1 has almost no ties) Y <- lapply(2:T_all, function(t) {     Yt <- (dutchcollege$Y[, , t] > 0) * 1     diag(Yt) <- NA     rownames(Yt) <- colnames(Yt) <- actor_names     Yt }) names(Y) <- paste0("t", 2:T_all)  # nodal covariates passed identically as sender and receiver X_node <- dutchcollege$X rownames(X_node) <- actor_names Xrow <- lapply(seq_along(Y), function(t) X_node) Xcol <- Xrow  # dyadic homophily indicators same_male <- outer(X_node[, "male"], X_node[, "male"], "==") * 1 same_smoker <- outer(X_node[, "smoker"], X_node[, "smoker"], "==") * 1 same_program <- outer(X_node[, "program"], X_node[, "program"], "==") * 1 Xdyad_one <- array(     0,     dim = c(n, n, 3),     dimnames = list(         actor_names,         actor_names,         c("same_male", "same_smoker", "same_program")     ) ) Xdyad_one[, , 1] <- same_male Xdyad_one[, , 2] <- same_smoker Xdyad_one[, , 3] <- same_program Xdyad <- lapply(seq_along(Y), function(t) Xdyad_one) sapply(Y, function(y) round(mean(y, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) #>   t2   t3   t4   t5   t6   t7  #> 0.40 0.52 0.47 0.49 0.63 0.51

title: Getting Started with lame
text: Networks trade, conflict, alliance, friendship, sanction share common inferential difficulty: tie two actors rarely independent ties around . central actor sends , attracts , shifts incentives every actor sharing neighbour. lame package fits Longitudinal Additive Multiplicative Effects models kind data. estimates covariate effects directed tie scale accounting sender heterogeneity, receiver heterogeneity, reciprocity, residual relational structure covariates alone capture. model decomposes tie three pieces. Every actor tendency send ties (aia_i) receive ties (bjb_j), reflecting active popular . actor also occupies latent position (uiu_i sender, vjv_j receiver) actors similar positions tend form similar tie patterns. Covariates shift baseline probability ties top actor-level pieces. observations span multiple periods, components can evolve time via AR(1) process – short “autoregressive order 1”, meaning period’s value slightly noisy copy previous period’s value (positions drift smoothly rather jumping around).

title: Getting Started with lame
text: Let’s fit model small longitudinal binary network one dyadic covariate (bilateral similarity score drives tie formation). truth intercept = -1.0 covariate effect beta = 0.7. intercept estimated -1.08 (truth -1.0) similarity_dyad 0.73 (truth 0.7). _dyad suffix coefficient name flags covariate pair-level quantity; sender-receiver-covariates carry _row _col suffixes respectively. remaining variance components describe residual actor-level dyad-level structure covariate alone explain: va: variance sender random effects, capturing much actors differ overall tendency send ties. vb: variance receiver random effects, capturing much differ tendency receive. cab: covariance sender receiver effects within actor, indicating whether prolific senders also frequent receivers. rho: within-dyad residual correlation, capturing reciprocity beyond additive effects covariates explain. note MCMC settings. three key parameters burn (iterations discarded burn-), nscan (post-burn-iterations kept inference), odens (thinning: keep every odens-th sample reduce autocorrelation). lame() runs two chains default, settings store nscan / odens = 100 / 5 = 20 draws per chain, 40 , keeps vignette quick build. defaults (burn = 500, nscan = 10000, odens = 25) length final run: 400 draws per chain, lame() compares across chains returns fit. Run defaults, example returns 800 draws continuation, every monitored R̂\hat R 1.005, estimates −1.08-1.08 0.730.73.
code: library(lame) set.seed(6886)  # three periods of a 25-actor directed network driven by a dyadic covariate n <- 25; T_periods <- 3 true_intercept <- -1.0 true_beta <- 0.7  # zero-padded names keep the input order under the alphabetical actor sort; # matching dimnames on Y and every covariate array keep them aligned actor_names <- sprintf("N%02d", seq_len(n))  X_list <- lapply(seq_len(T_periods), function(t) {     # [actor x actor x covariate] array; the slice name labels the coefficient     x <- matrix(rnorm(n * n), n, n)     array(         x,         dim = c(n, n, 1),         dimnames = list(actor_names, actor_names, "similarity")     ) }) Y_list <- lapply(seq_len(T_periods), function(t) {     # probit ties: tie probability pnorm(intercept + beta * x)     eta <- true_intercept + true_beta * X_list[[t]][, , 1]     Y <- matrix(rbinom(n * n, 1, pnorm(eta)), n, n)     diag(Y) <- NA # self-ties are undefined in a unipartite network     rownames(Y) <- colnames(Y) <- actor_names     Y })  # longitudinal AME model with the similarity covariate fit <- lame(     Y = Y_list,     Xdyad = X_list, # one similarity matrix per period     R = 2, # 2D latent space     family = "binary", # probit for 0/1 networks     burn = 20, # short burn-in for this example     nscan = 100, # short run for this example     odens = 5, # thinning     verbose = FALSE, # no progress output     plot = FALSE # no live diagnostic plots during sampling )  summary(fit) #>  #> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ────────────────────────────────────────────── #>  #> ── Call  #> Y ~ dyad(similarity) + a[i] + b[j] + rho*e[ji] + U[i,1:2] %*% V[j,1:2], family = 'binary' #>  #> ── Model  #> • Time periods: 3 #> • Family: binary #> • Mode: unipartite #> • Latent dimensions: 66%, 34% of the latent product #> ℹ Dimensions 1 and 2 have nearly equal strength, so their two axes are not well #> separated; read them together as a plane. #> ℹ Static fit: U, V, a and b are shared across the 3 periods, and per-period #> predictions vary through the per-period covariates. `dynamic_uv = TRUE` and #> `dynamic_ab = TRUE` let them vary over time. #>  #> ── Regression coefficients  #>                 Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat #> intercept         -1.083    0.052 -20.728       0   -1.179   -0.975 1.021 #> similarity_dyad    0.735    0.041  17.748       0     0.65    0.802 0.968 #>                 Threshold ESS     #> intercept            <NA>  40 *** #> similarity_dyad      <NA>  40 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use #>   the credible intervals. #>  #> ── Variance components  #>     Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold    ESS #> va     0.067    0.020 1.056        NA 40.000 #> cab   -0.007    0.015 1.023        NA 16.943 #> vb     0.055    0.018 0.985        NA 40.000 #> rho   -0.121    0.098 1.021        NA 12.410 #>   va = sender variance, cab = sender-receiver covariance, vb = receiver #>   variance, rho = dyadic correlation

Checkpoint / resume long runs. Pass max_seconds checkpoint_path run may hit wall-clock limit, continue resume_from; see ?lame_resume resume-cycle semantics. K-panel joint posterior. lame_multi() fits K parallel networks pools per-panel beta posteriors one precision-weighted shared posterior; see ?lame_multi. Memory-conscious loo(). save_log_lik = "chunked" streams log-score matrix disk instead RAM; read_log_lik() reads back, loo(fit) scores fits dcor = FALSE. See forecasting vignette. Multi-chain diagnostics. lame() runs two chains default (chains = 2) stores R̂\hat R fit$rhat; rhat_dynamic_beta() gives multivariate -chain R̂\hat R coefficient paths list fits run different seeds; see dynamic effects vignette. Held-predictive scoring. Mask dyads NA, refit (sampler imputes ), score masked cells evaluate_heldout(). binary outcomes returns Brier score log loss, plus AUROC PR-AUC precrec installed (AUROC alone pROC). code: ck <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") fit1 <- lame(     Y = Y_list,     Xdyad = X_list,     R = 2,     family = "binary",     nscan = 5000,     burn = 200,     odens = 25,     chains = 1, # a checkpoint is one chain     max_seconds = 30, # stop after 30 s wall clock     checkpoint_path = ck, # write state here     verbose = FALSE ) if (isTRUE(fit1$terminated_early)) {     # 2,000 more sweeps, keeping every 25th     fit2 <- lame(resume_from = ck, nscan = 2000) }

title: Longitudinal Additive and Multiplicative Effects Models for Networks
text: Longitudinal Additive Multiplicative Effects Models Networks Network ties – trade flows, friendships, alliances, sanctions – independent observations. actors send lot ties, receive lot, ties tend reciprocated, similar actors behave similarly. Run plain regression every (sender, receiver) pair coefficients standard errors come wrong. lame fits models account structure. Every actor gets sender effect (active ), receiver effect (popular ), position low-dimensional latent space soaks patterns covariates miss – homophily, clustering, transitivity. Covariates enter additively, just like regression, “longitudinal” part lets piece drift across time. package implements additive multiplicative effects (AME) framework developed Peter Hoff (popularised amen package), extends directions: lame() fits panel networks time-varying effects; ame() lame() handle bipartite (rectangular) networks alongside usual square case; sampler written C++ (Rcpp / RcppArmadillo) scale; fit exposes usual coef(), vcov(), confint(), predict(), fitted(), residuals(), simulate() methods, slots R modelling ecosystem like lm() glm(). also fast, MCMC-free empirical-Bayes estimator reports standard error every estimate – ame_als() / lame_als(), adapted Social Influence Regression estimator Minhas & Hoff (2025). Reach exploring, screening models, generating starting values, fitting large networks; use MCMC path full posterior ordinal, censored-binary fixed-rank families. New probit, latent space, AR(1)? vignette("lame") introduces context first fit.

title: Longitudinal Additive and Multiplicative Effects Models for Networks
text: Modes: cross-sectional (ame()), longitudinal (lame()), unipartite bipartite, six families. Dynamics: time-varying latent positions (dynamic_uv), sender/receiver effects (dynamic_ab), regression coefficients (dynamic_beta, per-block AR(1) / RW1 / RW2 / Matern 3/2), forecasting via predict(fit, h = K) (AR(1) RW1 coefficient paths). S3 methods MCMC ALS fits: coef(), vcov(), confint(), predict(), fitted(), residuals(), summary(), update(), simulate(), plus autoplot(). Ecosystem: broom::tidy() / glance(), modelsummary, as_draws() posterior / tidybayes, loo::loo() save_log_lik = TRUE (directed fits need dcor = FALSE, cell likelihood). Fit assessment: simulate() gof() posterior-predictive checks; gof_temporal() panels. Convergence scale: ame() lame() run two chains default (chains = 2) compare R-hat return; compute_mcmc_diagnostics() reports R-hat / ESS; lame_multi() several panels sharing coefficients; checkpoint/resume via checkpoint_path= lame_resume().

title: Longitudinal Additive and Multiplicative Effects Models for Networks
text: ame_als() / lame_als() fit model iterative block coordinate descent (alternating least squares / IRLS) – port Social Influence Regression estimator Minhas & Hoff (2025), implemented sir package. cover normal, binary poisson families, fit empirical-Bayes / variational estimator model samplers fit (see vignette("fast_estimation")). return point estimates standard errors rather posterior draws. Binary density: binary network panel whose density 0.2 0.8 fitted warning; sampler (ame() lame()) better choice. Dynamic fits: lame(..., method = "als") fits dynamic additive effects, selected dynamic coefficients, AR(1) latent factors (directed, symmetric, bipartite) Student-t ones (directed, symmetric). Normal, binary Poisson panels fitted dynamic empirical-Bayes estimator, standard errors coefficients, effects paths, variance components product cells. Tune als_max_iter, als_tol, als_stability. snap-shift kind (dynamic_uv_kind = "snap") fitted MCMC directed panels. Uncertainty: vcov() / confint() report Laplace standard errors every coefficient, every fit carries standard errors variance components, sender receiver effects latent positions. static fits, ame_als_bootstrap(), ame_als(..., bootstrap = N), adds block/parametric bootstrap intervals, confint() uses present.

title: Penalised ALS time-varying coefficient estimate — als_dynamic_beta
text: Y list \(T\) response matrices (3-D array third dimension time). Xdyad list \(T\) dyadic covariate arrays (\(n \times n \times p\), single \(n \times n\) matrix \(p=1\)). lambda Non-negative smoothing parameter. Default 0 (penalty, per-period OLS). intercept Logical; include intercept (default TRUE).

title: Penalised ALS time-varying coefficient estimate — als_dynamic_beta
text: list beta (\(p \times T\) matrix estimates; rows "intercept" names covariate slices Xdyad, "x1", "x2", ... slices unnamed; columns "t1", ..., "tT"), lambda, residual_ss (sum squared residuals across periods), intercept, call. Class "als_dynamic_beta".

title: Penalised ALS time-varying coefficient estimate — als_dynamic_beta
text: $$\min_{\beta_{1:T}} \sum_t \|y_t - X_t \beta_t\|^2 + \lambda   \sum_{t=2}^{T} \|\beta_t - \beta_{t-1}\|^2$$ \(\lambda = 0\) \(T\) independent per-period OLS fits. \(\lambda \\infty\) solution converges single pooled \(\beta\) (constant time).

title: Penalised ALS time-varying coefficient estimate — als_dynamic_beta
text: als_dynamic_beta regression-smoother; returned object carries time-varying \(\beta_t\) alone, additive (\(, b\)) multiplicative (\(U, V\)) AME components. therefore special case lame_als (always estimates full AME decomposition) special case lame(dynamic_beta = TRUE) (Bayesian AR(1) / RW1 / RW2 / Matern 3/2 state-space prior). Use want fast, point-, deterministic smoother coefficient path; use lame(dynamic_beta = ...) need full posterior uncertainty additive / multiplicative effects.

title: Penalised ALS time-varying coefficient estimate — als_dynamic_beta
code: set.seed(1) n <- 10; Tn <- 4 X <- replicate(Tn, array(rnorm(n*n*2), c(n, n, 2)), simplify = FALSE) beta_true <- rbind(seq(-1, 1, length.out = Tn), seq(0.5, -0.5, length.out = Tn)) Y <- vector("list", Tn) for (t in seq_len(Tn)) {   Yt <- X[[t]][, , 1] * beta_true[1, t] + X[[t]][, , 2] * beta_true[2, t] +         matrix(rnorm(n*n, 0, 0.2), n, n)   diag(Yt) <- NA   Y[[t]] <- Yt } fit_als <- als_dynamic_beta(Y, X, lambda = 0)     # per-period LS fit_smooth <- als_dynamic_beta(Y, X, lambda = 10) # smoother path

Theoretical Foundation: AME model decomposes network structure several components: $$y_{ij} = \beta'x_{ij} + a_i + b_j + u_i'v_j + \epsilon_{ij}$$ : \(\beta'x_{ij}\): Fixed effects dyadic/nodal covariates \(a_i\): Additive sender (row) effect node \(b_j\): Additive receiver (column) effect node j \(u_i'v_j\): Multiplicative interaction latent factors \(\epsilon_{ij}\): Dyadic error term (may correlated) specification generalizes social relations model (Warner et al. 1979) latent space models (Hoff et al. 2002) within unified framework. Multiplicative Effects (Latent Factors): R > 0, model includes R-dimensional latent factors: Asymmetric case: \(u_i, v_j \\mathbb{R}^R\) \(u_i'v_j\) interaction Symmetric case: \(u_i = v_i\) eigendecomposition \(ULU'\) Captures homophily, transitivity, community structure R chosen via model selection set 2-3 visualization Estimation Algorithm: model uses Gibbs sampler following updates: Sample latent Z given parameters (data augmentation non-normal families) Update regression coefficients \(\beta\) via g-prior conjugate update Update additive effects (,b) jointly \(\beta\) Update covariance \(\Sigma_{ab}\) inverse-Wishart Update multiplicative effects U,V via Gibbs Metropolis-Hastings Update dyadic correlation \(\rho\) via Metropolis-Hastings Update variance \(\sigma^2\) (continuous families) Standard Model Types: following data types/models available: "normal": normal AME model (identity link: \(E[Y] = \eta\)). what: When to use AME vs ERGM
title: AME model fitting routine — ame
text: AME ERGM complementary tools binary network analysis, direct substitutes. ERGM class exponential-family models built around explicit network statistics (counts edges, mutual ties, triangles, geometrically-weighted shared partners, ...). write statistics think matter, ERGM gives coefficients. ERGM excels substantive theory configurations drive tie formation. AME models latent homophily / heterogeneity directly via sender, receiver, multiplicative latent-factor effects. enumerate triadic terms; multiplicative-effects rank R captures higher-order structure (clustering, transitivity, hub patterns) implicitly. AME excels () dyadic / nodal covariates whose effects want interpret cleanly without ERGM degeneracy, (b) higher-order structure "nuisance" want absorb parameterise, (c) need posterior distribution predictions forecasting imputation. Practical guidance: research question "nodes share attribute X tend form triangles together?", reach ERGM's gwesp. research question "controlling unobserved sender / receiver heterogeneity latent clustering, effect dyadic covariate X?", reach AME. R = 0 additive-case social relations model (Warner, Kenny, Stoto 1979); R >= 1 adds latent space.

code: # \donttest{ # twelve periods supply the ten resampling blocks the block scheme needs Y <- replicate(12, { m <- matrix(rnorm(225), 15, 15); diag(m) <- NA; m },                simplify = FALSE) fit <- lame_als(Y, R = 1, family = "normal", verbose = FALSE) # post-hoc bootstrap of an existing fit: bt <- ame_als_bootstrap(fit, R = 50, type = "block",                             seed = 1, verbose = FALSE) # equivalent one-shot call: # fit_b <- lame_als(Y, R = 1, family = "normal", verbose = FALSE, #                   bootstrap = 50, bootstrap_type = "block", #                   bootstrap_seed = 1) print(bt) #>  #> Bootstrap results: fast AME estimator #> Type: block | Family: normal | Replicates: 50/50 valid #>  #>           Estimate Boot SE    2.5%  97.5% #> intercept  -0.0021  0.0216 -0.0425 0.0458 #>  #> beta, a, b and variance components aggregate directly; U/V are #> Procrustes-aligned. #> Block resample of 12 blocks: the interval ends are the 1.1% and 98.9% quantiles #> of the replicates. #> Analytic standard errors and intervals for va, cab, vb, where the bootstrap #> gives none: slice resampling holds the actors fixed, and the sampling #> variability of the variances of the actor effects is that over actors. #> Analytic standard errors and intervals for a, b, U, V, where the bootstrap #> gives none: the effects of this estimator are shrunk toward their prior mean, #> and the replicates of a resample vary around the shrunk estimates, not around #> the effects. #> Analytic standard errors and intervals for ve, where the bootstrap gives none: #> the refit to resampled slices, which repeat some and omit others, absorbs more #> of the noise than the original fit, so the replicate residual variances sit #> below the estimate. #> `type = "parametric"` gives intervals for them. # }

title: Held-out predictive evaluation for an ame / lame fit — evaluate_heldout
code: # \donttest{ set.seed(1) n <- 25; Y <- matrix(rbinom(n*n, 1, 0.3), n, n); diag(Y) <- NA rownames(Y) <- colnames(Y) <- paste0("a", sprintf("%02d", 1:n)) # mask 20% of dyads mask <- matrix(FALSE, n, n) obs_idx <- which(!is.na(Y)) set.seed(1) mask[sample(obs_idx, floor(0.2 * length(obs_idx)))] <- TRUE Y_train <- Y; Y_train[mask] <- NA # chains = 1 keeps the example short; the default runs two chains and compares them fit <- ame(Y_train, R = 0, family = "binary",            burn = 15, nscan = 60, odens = 5, verbose = FALSE, plot = FALSE, chains = 1) y_pred <- predict(fit, type = "response") evaluate_heldout(Y, y_pred, mask, family = "binary") #>   n_eval     auroc     auprc    brier   logloss #> 1    120 0.4706328 0.2497777 0.195101 0.5799574 # }

title: Probability-integral-transform calibration check for h-step forecasts — forecast_pit
text: fit fitted lame lame_robust object trained first T - h periods (function refit; user responsible train/forecast split). y_future list length h held-observed matrices, one per forecast period. shape fitted actor grid. Named periods aligned shared actors; unshared actors missing outcomes excluded. Unipartite self cells excluded symmetric networks score unordered dyad . Bipartite grids retain cells whose row column positions coincide. h forecast horizon (length y_future). Inferred length(y_future) supplied. n_draws Number posterior draws use forecast. Default uses stored draws. newdata Future dyadic covariate arrays passed forecaster. Required robust fits contain dyadic covariates, predict.lame_robust(). newdesign Full prepared future designs, including nodal roles. Supported ordinary lame fits. newexposure Future Poisson exposures, one per horizon. Defaults last fitted exposure. Zero exposure defines degenerate zero-count law.

title: Probability-integral-transform calibration check for h-step forecasts — forecast_pit
text: list class forecast_pit components pit (numeric vector), ks_stat (KS statistic Uniform), ks_p (NA; dependent-network null reference unavailable), cover_95 (fraction PIT values [0.025, 0.975]), matched draw_index, predictive cdf_lower/cdf_upper, scored actor/period cells. Network cells need independent. KS statistic, histogram coverage descriptive. global model-adequacy p-value reported without calibrated joint network reference. ks_inference records restriction.

title: Probability-integral-transform calibration check for h-step forecasts — forecast_pit
text: Workflow: fit periods 1:(T - h), forecast h steps ahead, score held-T - h + 1 : T observations. Returns numeric vector PIT values (one per observed dyad held-periods), plus one-row summary Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic Uniform(0, 1) fraction--observed-dyads coverage diagnostic. Families. family = "normal", PIT averages Gaussian CDF matched predictor residual-variance draws. discrete families ("binary", "poisson", "ordinal") randomised PIT Czado, Gneiting & Held (2009) used. Poisson forecasts integrate Gaussian observation effect future exposure. Ordinal scoring requires saved explicit posterior cutpoints; data-induced joint rank simulation define fixed future threshold law. rank families ("cbin", "frn") PIT implemented; function returns NULL informational note. Robust fits lame_robust() use genuine future latent states, matched persistent pair precisions Gaussian transient Student residual CDF. Fitted temporary observation precisions never reused future outcomes. Plotting. companion plot() method returned object renders histogram uniform reference line. Use ggplot2::ggplot(pit$pit) + geom_histogram() custom plots.

title: Probability-integral-transform calibration check for h-step forecasts — forecast_pit
text: Czado, C., Gneiting, T., & Held, L. (2009). Predictive model assessment count data. Biometrics, 65(4), 1254-1261.

title: Visualize goodness-of-fit statistics for AME and LAME models — gof_plot
text: Overview: Goodness--fit (GOF) assessment crucial network models standard residual diagnostics often inadequate capturing network dependencies. function implements posterior predictive checking : Computing key network statistics observed data Generating multiple networks model's posterior predictive distribution Computing statistics simulated networks Visualizing comparison identify model inadequacies Network Statistics Evaluated: unipartite (square) networks: sd.row (-degree heterogeneity) Standard deviation row means. High values indicate substantial variation active nodes senders/initiators. model underestimates , may missing important sender effects covariates. sd.col (-degree heterogeneity) Standard deviation column means. High values indicate substantial variation node popularity receivers. Underestimation suggests missing receiver effects popularity-related covariates. dyad.dep (Reciprocity/Mutuality) Correlation Y[,j] Y[j,]. Positive values indicate reciprocity (mutual ties likely). AME model captures dyadic correlation parameter rho. Poor fit points adjusting dcor parameter. triad.dep (Transitivity/Clustering) Measures tendency triadic closure (friend friend friend). Calculated correlation Y[,j] sum(Y[,k]*Y[k,j])/sqrt(n-2). AME captures multiplicative effects (U,V). Poor fit suggests increasing latent dimension R. bipartite (rectangular) networks: Rows columns different node sets, panels labelled row column rather sender receiver. sd.row (Row degree heterogeneity) Standard deviation row means. Indicates heterogeneity actively row nodes connect column nodes. sd.col (Column degree heterogeneity) Standard deviation column means. Indicates heterogeneity often column nodes connected row nodes. four.cycles (Bipartite clustering) Count 4-cycles (rectangular paths A1-B1-A2-B2-A1). High values indicate pairs Type nodes tend connect Type B nodes. Used families structural zeros, including binary outcomes. four.cycle.dep (Weighted bipartite dependence) Gaussian outcomes, averages products centered, standardized cell values around fully observed rectangles. measures weighted dependence; nonzero-edge count fixed observed-cell pattern. Interpretation Guide: Histogram plots (static models): Dashed black vertical line: observed statistic value (dual-encoded colour linetype) Grey histogram: distribution posterior predictive simulations Good fit: dashed line falls within bulk histogram Poor fit: dashed line tail outside distribution Common model inadequacies solutions: Observed sd.row/sd.col high Model underestimates degree heterogeneity. Solutions: Add row/column covariates (Xrow, Xcol), enable random effects (rvar=TRUE, cvar=TRUE), increase variance. Observed dyad.dep outside distribution Reciprocity captured well. Solutions: positive reciprocity, ensure dcor=TRUE. negative, consider transformation different family. Observed triad.dep high Clustering/transitivity underestimated. Solutions: Increase latent dimension R, add network covariates capture homophily, consider including community structure covariates. Multiple statistics showing poor fit Fundamental model misspecification. Solutions: Change family, add missing covariates, consider different model class. Mathematical Details: posterior predictive p-value statistic s : $$p = P(s(Y_{rep}) \geq s(Y_{obs}) | Y_{obs})$$ Y_rep drawn posterior predictive distribution. Values near 0 1 indicate poor fit. function visualizes full distribution rather just p-values richer diagnostics. Customization: function accepts custom GOF statistics model's custom_gof argument. automatically included plot. Custom statistics capture network features important specific application. Computational Notes: GOF computation involves simulating multiple networks, can computationally intensive. model uses networks simulated MCMC gof=TRUE specified. post-hoc GOF, use gof() function generates new simulations. Good model fit indicated : Observed statistics fall within central 95% posterior predictive distributions systematic patterns /underestimation across statistics Custom statistics (provided) also show adequate fit longitudinal models, observed trajectories track within credible bands

title: Gibbs update for additive effects covariance — rSab_fc
text: vector row random effects (additive sender effects) b vector column random effects (additive receiver effects) Sab0 prior scale matrix. Convention (Hoff/amen): Sab0 passed raw; inverse-Wishart scale used internally \(\eta_0 \cdot Sab0\), prior mean Sab \(\eta_0 Sab0/(\eta_0-3) \approx Sab0\) prior mode \(\eta_0 Sab0/(\eta_0+3)\). Every call site package (ame() unipartite bipartite, lame() unipartite bipartite, raSab_bin/cbin/frn joint updates) passes Sab0 raw convention, given prior$Sab0 means prior everywhere. Default diag(2) (weakly informative). eta0 prior degrees freedom prior distribution. Default 4, smallest integer giving finite prior mean 2x2 covariance. rvar logical: row variance updated? (default TRUE) cvar logical: column variance updated? (default TRUE) symmetric logical: symmetric network? (default FALSE) center Logical: supplied actor effects constrained sum zero? , remove one degree freedom covariance update. Defaults FALSE unconstrained effects. tiny variance margin switched (rvar cvar FALSE) keeps: 1e-8 unit response (default 1e-8, value link-fixed latent scale).

title: Multivariate R-hat for dynamic_beta coefficient paths — rhat_dynamic_beta
text: chain \(c\), let \(\beta^{(c)}_t \\mathbb{R}^T\) path. \(m\) chains \(n\) iterations per chain, define $$W_k = \tfrac{1}{m}\sum_c S_c^{(k)}, \quad         B_k = \tfrac{n}{m-1}\sum_c (\bar\beta_c^{(k)} - \bar\beta^{(k)})(\bar\beta_c^{(k)} - \bar\beta^{(k)})'$$ \(S_c^{(k)}\) within-chain sample covariance path \(k\) chain \(c\). \(V_k = ((n-1)/n) W_k + ((m+1)/(mn)) B_k\) \(\hat R_k^{mvt} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(W_k^{-1} V_k)}\). nearly degenerate covariances add tiny ridge \(W_k\).

title: Multivariate R-hat for dynamic_beta coefficient paths — rhat_dynamic_beta

title: lame 1.3.4
text: CRAN release: 2026-08-04 handful Gibbs samplers helpers adapted amen rewritten underlying published methods, package carries derived code stays MIT license. Fixed prior-scaling bug silently collapse latent factors asymmetric ame() fits R > 0; fits now match amen. dynamic_ab fits carry per-period posterior SDs, ab_plot(fit, plot_type = "ribbon") draws real credible band. documented options now say: log_lik_method = "augmented", gof(nsim = NULL) (uses draws), bootstrap error bars ab_plot() ame_als fits. Dropped unused argument fixed stale help text. Fitting longer leaves .Random.seed behind touches options(warn). Fixed Rd markup flagged CRAN. Time-varying coefficients (dynamic_beta) compose freely multiplicative latent factors (R > 0) additive sender/receiver effects, every family network type. Coefficients can follow AR(1), random-walk, Matern dynamics, predict() carries drift forecasts. netify objects can passed straight ame(), lame(), ALS fitters; network’s symmetric attribute honored automatically, named covariates aligned Y actor. Set posterior_opts = list(save_UV = TRUE) keep per-draw latent factors (bipartite mixing matrix), latent_positions(), uv_plot(), goodness--fit tools report posterior uncertainty directly. Symmetric fits now store V_samples (U L per draw) alongside U_samples, per-draw latent similarity U L U' reconstructable via simulate_posterior(fit, "UV"). summary() lame fit exposes coefficient table $coefficients, matching summary.ame broom/lm idiom. ## Known limitations Bipartite fit$U / fit$V single posterior draw (rotation unidentified); use fit$YPM reconstruct_UVPM() stable multiplicative structure. bipartite dynamic_uv path, latent persistence rho_uv weakly identified – read qualitatively. unipartite path unaffected. # lame 1.2.0 Cleaned ALS support documentation. Raised lame(method = "als") iteration cap exposed dynamic ALS convergence component traces. Stabilized dynamic-UV MCMC normalizing raw U/V coordinate scale, centering additive row/column effects, pooling sparse additive effects toward prior mean, carrying ALS fits MCMC als_start_vals(). # lame 1.1.0 ## New features Fast, MCMC-free estimation via ame_als() lame_als(): alternating least squares / IRLS point estimator normal, binary, Poisson families. Supports parametric-bootstrap sandwich standard errors full S3 method set (coef(), vcov(), confint(), predict(), tidy(), glance(), diagnostic plots). # lame 1.0.0 ## Initial CRAN Submission ### Features Cross-sectional network analysis via ame() support 6 distributional families: normal, binary, ordinal, Poisson, censored binary, fixed rank nomination. Longitudinal network analysis via lame() dynamic additive multiplicative effects modeled AR(1) processes. Support unipartite (square) bipartite (rectangular) network structures. Covariate support: dyadic (Xdyad), row (Xrow), column (Xcol) covariates automatic design matrix construction. S3 methods: print(), summary(), coef(), vcov(), confint(), predict(), fitted(), residuals(), simulate(), plot(). Visualization functions: trace_plot(), gof_plot(), ab_plot(), uv_plot() MCMC diagnostics model assessment. Goodness--fit via posterior predictive checks gof(). C++ acceleration via Rcpp RcppArmadillo core sampling routines. Handles changing actor compositions across time periods.
